PRESCHOOL · AGE 3 · CLASS 2

Numbers & Counting (1–10)

Age 3 YearsClass Preschool 2Subjects Counting & number recognition

Ten counting cards, printable number sheets to solve and a pocketful of real-life counting ideas. This class follows Alphabet & Letter Sounds on the preschool path — same calm pacing, now with numbers.

You do not need to reach ten today. Counting one to three with a pointing finger is a genuine maths lesson at three; five is a triumph; ten is a party. Let your child set the pace.

Start Today’s Class ↓Grown-up nearby, little one on the lap or hopping like a frog — both work.
TODAY’S CLASS

How today’s class works.

Four little steps, in any order that suits you: a welcome from your teacher, the number cards, solving the number sheets together, an off-screen hunt, and a warm goodbye. Stop after any step — that is a complete class, and there is never a score at the end.

  2. 2 Learn the numbers
  3. 3 Solve the sheets
  4. 4 Take it off screen
  5. 5 Class complete
TEACHER WELCOME

LEARN THE NUMBERS

Ten counting cards, from 1 to 10.

Every card shows a big numeral, the number word and the right number of things to count. Use the arrows to wander through them in order — or tap a group below to count just a few at a time. Counting to five and stopping is a complete visit.

Card 1 of 10
Or simply scroll: all 10 cards are below.
SOLVE THE SHEETS — ON PAPER OR ON SCREEN

Solve the number sheets together.

The ten number cards print two to a page, straight from your browser. Printed, cut and counted, they are the class’s real worksheets — and on screen, every card page can be drawn on directly.

  1. 01

    Print the cards

    Open the printable cards and print all ten, two to a page. Cut them out together, counting up as each number is cut.

  2. 02

    Count the pictures

    Each card carries its own little group — one apple, two ducks, three cats. Count the pictures aloud together before naming the numeral.

  3. 03

    Build the staircase

    Lay the cards in a line from 1 to 10 on the floor. Gaps and swaps are welcome — putting right a wobbly staircase is the thinking work.

  4. 04

    Match card to things

    Pick a card and find its count in the house: one spoon, five ladybugs on a page. Then trace the numeral on the card page with the Write & Color layer.

Open the printable cards ↗Draw on the cards on screen ↗

Every card page has a Write & Color layer: your child can draw right on the card with a finger, a stylus or the mouse, then save the finished work. Nothing is uploaded anywhere.

TAKE IT OFF SCREEN

Counting that lives in your house.

Real counting sticks best away from the screen, in short playful moments with things you already own. Pick one of these — two minutes is plenty — and follow your child’s lead.

Count three toys

  • Line up three favourite toys and count them slowly, pointing at each one.
  • One number per toy is the whole game — the toys do not need to sit still for long.

Count steps together

  • Stairs, garden steps, hallway hops — count them out loud as you go.
  • “One... two... three!” with every step turns any staircase into a counting game.

Count fingers

  • Hold up one hand and count each finger slowly — five is the hand number.
  • Finish with a high-five: “Five! High-five!” The clap makes it stick.

Count blocks as you stack

  • Stack blocks one by one and say the number every time one lands.
  • When the tower falls, count again — rebuilds are free extra lessons in disguise.

Five in a row

  • Put five safe objects in a row — pebbles, spoons, cars — and point to each while counting.
  • A straight line helps your child see what has been counted and what is left.

Stay close, keep it playful and stop while it is still fun. There is nothing to finish here.

A NOTE FROM THE PRINCIPAL

For the grown-ups.

At three, counting is rhythm, not arithmetic: one number per object, said slowly, is the entire curriculum. If your child skips a number or recounts the same duck twice, that is completely on track — the pointing-and-saying skill grows through play, and every gentle recount is real practice. The games here give calm feedback with no scores, and every dot group in Count and Match is mathematically exact, because counting accuracy matters more than decoration.

TIPS FOR PARENTS

How to use this class.

Sit together for the card viewing, and let your child do the pointing and the tapping in the games — even when the answer looks obvious to you. The finger teaches the eye, and being the one who knows is the fun part.

Count everything slowly, with one number per thing: apples, ducks, fingers, stairs. If a count goes wrong, simply start again from one with a smile — nobody is keeping score, least of all the cards.

Age 3 is a guide, not a deadline. If today’s class was two numbers and a staircase, today’s class was a success.

    LEARNING PATH LESSON · NUMBERS 1–10 · AGES 3–4 YEARS

    One Apple — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

    This lesson starts counting where counting actually starts: with one. Your child meets the numeral, the word and one shiny apple, then spends the day discovering that everything has a one — one head, one tummy, one favourite chair.

    What is this?

    One means a single thing — just the one, and no more. On the card it looks like a big red numeral, the word one, and a single smiling apple: the whole idea of one-ness drawn in three pieces your child can point at.

    What does it mean?

    Before children count groups, they notice singles — and one is the only number a three-year-old can verify by feel: one hand closed, one nose tapped, one apple on the card. That certainty is the confidence every later number borrows.

    What does the child need to know?

    Your child needs to know: one means a single thing, the numeral 1 is its picture, and singles are everywhere — one spoon, one shoe, one doorbell. Spotting one against many is the milestone; everything past it is repetition.

    Why this matters

    One is the seed the whole number line grows from: two is one and one more, three is one more again. A child who owns one deeply — not just recites it — has the unit idea installed before the bigger numbers arrive.

    What it teaches

    One-to-one noticing, numeral recognition, singular-to-plural language (one apple, many apples), pointing precision, and the pride of a first number fully owned.

    Words to learn

    oneapplesinglefirstpointalone

    Say this to your child

    “"Look — the number one! And here is one apple, all by itself. Can you touch it once? One tap — one apple! Now find me one thing in this room... one spoon! One! Everything has a one somewhere — can you find another?"”

    Step by step

    1. Show the card and ask what number is hiding on it — then say one together, slowly, while a finger lands on the big numeral.
    2. Touch the apple once — a single, deliberate tap — and say one apple. The one-touch rule starts here and never changes.
    3. Sweep the room for ones: one nose, one cup, one door. Touch each find once and whisper the word.
    4. Hold up one finger, then two, then one again — let your child show you one with their hand until the finger pops up on request.
    5. Put one block on the table and ask how many. Then add more and ask again — one stays one until a second block arrives, and your child just proved it.

    Look closer at the picture

    Look at the card together: where is the big red numeral 1? Where is the word one? And how many apples are on the card — count them with one slow touch. The numeral, the word and the single apple all say the same thing.

    Ask your child

    "How many apples do you see?" "Can you touch it just once?" "Can you show me one finger?" "What else comes in ones — look around?" "Is one more than none?" — real questions with touchable answers.

    What your child can say or do

    Your child may announce "one!" at every single object for a day — one sock, one biscuit, one extremely plural pile of blocks. Counting errors here go the friendly way: calling things one is the enthusiasm phase, and it passes into precision.

    Out in the real world

    Ones fill every day: one sun in the sky, one belly button at bath time, one key for the door, one child in the car seat. Name them as you meet them — each one named is the number rehearsed in the wild.

    Try it together

    One-and-only basket: fill a basket with pairs and singles — two spoons, one cup, two socks, one car — and ask your child to fish out only the ones. Then reverse: hand them the cup and ask how many. The sorting is the game; the answering is the maths.

    Understanding check

    Hold up the card and ask how many apples, then hold up a finger and ask how many. Two right answers with one-touch pointing — that is the number landed, unit and all.

    Parent tips

    Accept every "one!" happily, even the wrong ones, then model the count yourself: touch the objects once, slowly. Correction is not needed when demonstration is available — and demonstration always is.

    Staying safe

    Counting hunts stay floor-level and finger-sized: nothing small enough to swallow joins the game, especially with a baby sibling around. One is a fine number for biscuits, too — but sitting down for eating, always.

    This lesson pairs with the One Apple flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Numbers 1–10.

    LEARNING PATH LESSON · NUMBERS 1–10 · AGES 3–4 YEARS

    Two Ducks — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

    This lesson teaches the beat of counting: your child points at the first duck and says one, points at the second and says two — one number per object, in order, the rhythm every count from now on will dance to.

    What is this?

    Two means one and then one more. On the card: a pair of yellow ducks, the word two and a big numeral 2 — each duck waiting for its own number, in its own turn.

    What does it mean?

    Counting is not reciting — it is matching numbers to things, one each. The ducks make that visible: miss a duck and the count comes out wrong; double-tap one and it comes out wrong differently. The errors teach the rule better than the successes.

    What does the child need to know?

    Your child needs: two is one and one more, each duck gets one number all its own, and doing the pointing and the saying at once is real brain juggling — it is fine to tap while the grown-up counts, or count while the grown-up taps.

    Why this matters

    One-to-one correspondence — one number, one object, no leftovers — is the foundation under all arithmetic. The duck pair is its smallest, kindest version: two objects, two words, one satisfying click when they match.

    What it teaches

    One-to-one correspondence, pointing accuracy, sequencing (first duck, then second), pair-vocabulary (two shoes, two hands, two eyes), and rhythm — counting has a beat, and this is where children first feel it.

    Words to learn

    twoduckspairpointnextboth

    Say this to your child

    “"Two ducks! Let’s say hello to each one — this duck is one... and this duck is two. Two ducks! Can you tap them? Now find two of something — two ears! Tap one, tap the other: one, two. Every duck gets its own number, just like that."”

    Step by step

    1. Show the card and ask how many ducks are waiting — then count them together, one tap per duck: one... two.
    2. Count again with your child pointing and you saying the numbers, then swap: they say them, you tap. Both halves of the job need practising.
    3. Go tapping for twos: two ears, two shoes, two hands, two wheels on the trike. Touch each half of the pair as you count it.
    4. Line up two blocks and count them left to right, then swap their places and count again — two stays two no matter where the ducks wander.
    5. Finish with the pair test: hold up both hands and ask how many thumbs. Tap them together — one, two — and let your child take the last count alone.

    Look closer at the picture

    Look at the card together: how many ducks, and what colour are they? Point to each one as you count — one duck, then the other duck. Can your child find both number-pictures on the card, the 2 and the word two?

    Ask your child

    "How many ducks are on the card?" "Can you tap each duck once?" "What else comes in twos on your body?" "If one duck swam away, how many would be left?" — questions a three-year-old can answer with a tap, a giggle or a confident shout.

    What your child can say or do

    Your child may march around tapping pairs and announcing "two!" — shoes, knees, eyes, biscuits. Expect skips and double-taps at first; the tap-and-say coordination assembles itself over days, and every wrong count is doing real teaching work.

    Out in the real world

    Pairs run through the whole day: two sleeves, two welly boots by the door, two slices of toast, two eyes blinking in the mirror. Name the twos as they happen — each pair counted is the rhythm rehearsed.

    Try it together

    Pair hunt: hide four objects around the room — two cups, two spoons — and send your child to fetch the two that match. Bringing back a pair is one-to-one counting with a delivery job attached.

    Understanding check

    Ask for a two-count tomorrow on anything at hand — two biscuits, two blocks. If each object gets exactly one tap and one number, the rule has landed; if the count sprints ahead of the taps, tap along together for a few days.

    Parent tips

    Slow is the whole trick: your counting pace should match your tapping pace exactly. If hands and words tangle, take one job each — your taps, their numbers — and swap tomorrow. The coordination is the milestone, not the answer.

    Staying safe

    Tapping targets stay big and soft — ears, cups, cushions — and small countables stay out of baby siblings’ reach. Ducks on the card float safely; real bathtime ducks get counted sitting down, never standing in the water.

    This lesson pairs with the Two Ducks flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Numbers 1–10.

    LEARNING PATH LESSON · NUMBERS 1–10 · AGES 3–4 YEARS

    Three Cats — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

    This lesson gives your child their first middle-sized number: three. Small enough to trust at a glance, big enough that pointing still matters — and the cats are close enough together that every touch lands somewhere new.

    What is this?

    Three is one, then one more, then one more again. On the card: a trio of orange cats, the word three and a big green numeral 3 — enough cats to count, few enough to check the answer with a single look.

    What does it mean?

    Three is where counting starts to feel like an amount rather than a word: a trio is visibly more than a pair. Children also meet their own age here — being three is a very fine thing to have in common with a number.

    What does the child need to know?

    Your child needs: three comes after two, each cat gets one touch and one number, and three stays three even when the cats trade places. Recounting after a mix-up is not failing — it is the actual skill.

    Why this matters

    Seeing three without counting and counting three by touch meet on this card, and the shuffle-and-recount game quietly teaches a deep truth: number belongs to the group, not the arrangement. That is conservation of number, met in play.

    What it teaches

    Counting accuracy at the edge of a glance, touch-to-word coordination, arranging and rearranging small groups, and the age-pride connection — I am three, and three is on the card.

    Words to learn

    threecatsmorecountgroupmiddle

    Say this to your child

    “"Three cats! Count them with me — one, two, three. Then touch each cat once as you go. Now let’s make a three of our own — three blocks in a row. Count them... shuffle them... count again! Three every time. Three is a proper amount!"”

    Step by step

    1. Show the card and ask how many cats came to visit — then count them together, one touch per cat, in any order your child chooses.
    2. Count again the other way round and land on three twice — arriving at the same number twice is the most convincing maths there is.
    3. Build a three: line up three toys, count them, then rearrange — tower, row, circle — and count after every rebuild. Three survives them all.
    4. Play show-me-three: your child fetches three of something — three leaves, three pegs, three crackers — and you count the haul out loud together.
    5. Finish with the body: three jumps, three claps, three roars — a cat number deserves a cat sound at the end.

    Look closer at the picture

    Look at the card together: how many cats, and what colour are they? Touch each cat once as you count. Where is the big green numeral 3? Where is the word three? The cats and the numeral agree.

    Ask your child

    "How many cats?" "Can you touch each one once?" "Is three more than two — how do you know?" "Can you hop three times?" "How old are you — and what is on the card?" — answered with touches, hops and a very proud number.

    What your child can say or do

    Your child may count everything in threes for a week, announce their age with new authority — "I am THREE!" — and build threes out of crackers, cars and pebbles. Recounts that land somewhere new are normal and useful: say the count again slowly, together.

    Out in the real world

    Threes are everywhere once named: three wheels on a trike, three traffic lights, three fish fingers on the plate, three bears in the story. Count them as you meet them — each real three is the card rehearsed.

    Try it together

    Three-coin tea party: three cups, three spoons, three guests (any toys will attend). Your child sets each place — one spoon per cup, one per guest — which is one-to-one counting with a whole party riding on it.

    Understanding check

    Scatter three blocks differently tomorrow and ask for the count: a confident three means the number has detached from the layout — the deepest thing this card teaches.

    Parent tips

    Let your child choose the counting order; ownership speeds learning. If a recount lands on four, count again yourself at snail pace — no correction, just a model — and let the cats set the tempo.

    Staying safe

    Counting snacks get eaten sitting down, and small countables — coins, pegs, pebbles — stay away from babies and out of mouths. The tea-party guests should be too big to swallow; toys have a way of ending up tasted at this age.

    This lesson pairs with the Three Cats flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Numbers 1–10.

    LEARNING PATH LESSON · NUMBERS 1–10 · AGES 3–4 YEARS

    Four Cars — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

    This lesson takes counting past the glance: four is where pointing and patience start pulling real weight. Your child counts the cars one careful touch at a time, then parks fours all over the house — four wheels, four corners, four crackers.

    What is this?

    Four is three and one more. On the card: four little blue cars, the word four and a big numeral 4 — a tidy parking lot for a careful count.

    What does it mean?

    At four, children meet the honest work of counting: the answer no longer arrives by looking, and double-counts happen. That is not failure — noticing the count went wrong IS the number sense developing, and it deserves applause.

    What does the child need to know?

    Your child needs: four comes after three, each car gets exactly one touch, and four can feel like "just lots" on some days. Parking the cars in rows makes counting kind — tidy beats scattered at every stage of learning to count.

    Why this matters

    Four sits at the edge of what a three-year-old can see at a glance, which makes it the perfect training number: easy on good days, countable on all days. The square layout quietly introduces rows and corners — early maths furniture.

    What it teaches

    Touch-counting past the glance zone, working memory (holding the count in mind), arranging objects in rows and squares, and the growing patience that longer counts quietly build.

    Words to learn

    fourcarssquarecornerrowmore

    Say this to your child

    “"One, two, three, four — four cars! Let’s touch each one as we count. Beep beep! Now park four cars of your own — count them into their spots. If a count goes wonky, no worries — park them again and start from one. Four careful touches, four cars!"”

    Step by step

    1. Show the card and ask how many cars are parked on it — then count together, one touch per car, taking the corners in order.
    2. Park your own four: four blocks or four toy cars in a square, touched and counted one by one — then drive one away and count what is left.
    3. Hunt fours through the house: four chair legs, four wheels on the big car, four corners of the rug. Touch as you count, every time.
    4. Try the two-and-two trick: count the top two cars, then the bottom two, then all four together — two little counts making one big one.
    5. Finish with four claps, four stamps and a four-wheeled parade around the rug — counting that arrives from the legs up.

    Look closer at the picture

    Look at the card together: how many little cars, and what colour are they? Touch each car once as you count from one to four. Where is the big numeral 4, and where is the word four?

    Ask your child

    "How many cars are on the card?" "Can you touch each one once?" "How many wheels does your favourite car have?" "Is four more than three?" "Can you clap four times?" — answered with touches, claps and engine noises.

    What your child can say or do

    Your child may count four soup ladles, four stair steps and four everything — with occasional five-and-six answers when enthusiasm outruns the fingers. The four-means-lots phase is genuine progress wearing a messy coat.

    Out in the real world

    Fours wait in every room: four table legs, four candles on a birthday cake, four socks pegged on the line, four seasons named at bedtime. Each one counted is a repetition of the card.

    Try it together

    Parking lot: chalk or tape a four-space square on the floor and let your child drive one car into each space, counting as they park. A full lot means four — and every empty space asks the question out loud.

    Understanding check

    Ask for four of something tomorrow — four blocks into your hand: a counted, touched, correct four means the number has moved in. A miscount means the parking lot needs another week of business, which is fine.

    Parent tips

    Keep counting pace slower than your child’s enthusiasm — the finger must arrive with the word. Rows and tidy squares help small counters more than any explanation: park the objects neatly, and the numbers behave.

    Staying safe

    Toy cars with real rolling wheels stay on the floor, not tables where they launch from. Counting snacks get cut small and eaten sitting down — and the parking lot keeps walkways clear, for toddlers and grown-up shins alike.

    This lesson pairs with the Four Cars flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Numbers 1–10.

    LEARNING PATH LESSON · NUMBERS 1–10 · AGES 3–4 YEARS

    Five Ladybugs — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

    This lesson lands on the number your child carries on the end of each arm: five. Five ladybugs to touch, five fingers to wiggle, and the perfect place for a first proper counting session to finish.

    What is this?

    Five is four and one more — a whole hand. On the card: five red ladybugs, the word five and a big numeral 5 — little counting stations waiting for their taps.

    What does it mean?

    Five is the first number with a body part of its own: the hand. Children can check a five against their own fingers, which makes it the first number that verifies itself — count the bugs, then count the hand, same answer.

    What does the child need to know?

    Your child needs: five comes after four, each ladybug gets one touch, and five matches one whole hand. Reaching five in order — wobbles allowed — is a proud, complete day’s work, not a warm-up.

    Why this matters

    Finger-counting is the training wheels of arithmetic: it makes numbers touchable, portable and always available. Five is the anchor point — once a child trusts five, six-to-ten become five-and-some-more, and the number line folds in half.

    What it teaches

    Finger counting, touch accuracy at five objects, counting a group that arrives in rows (a quiet prelude to adding), and the satisfaction of a finish line reached by pointing.

    Words to learn

    fiveladybugshandfingersrowsfinish

    Say this to your child

    “"Five ladybugs! Let’s count them — one touch each: one, two, three, four, five. Now count your fingers — the same number! Five ladybugs, five fingers. High-five! Five is a whole hand, and today you counted all the way there."”

    Step by step

    1. Show the card and ask how many ladybugs landed on it — then count together, one gentle touch per ladybug.
    2. Hold up one hand and count the fingers — one to five, thumb first — then match each finger to a ladybug on the card, one for one.
    3. Seal the count with a high-five: five! The slap makes the number arrive in the palm as well as the ears.
    4. Set the table for five: five pegs in a row, five blocks, five pom-poms — touched and counted into place, one per tap.
    5. Finish with five jumps, five claps and one enormous high-five — the hand number deserves the full-body send-off.

    Look closer at the picture

    Look at the card together: how many red ladybugs are visiting it? Touch each one as you count to five. Find the big numeral 5 and the word five — then hold up your hand and count its five fingers too.

    Ask your child

    "How many ladybugs are on the card?" "Can you touch every one of them?" "How many fingers on one hand?" "Is five more than four — how could we check?" "Can you give me a high-five?" — every answer ends in a slap.

    What your child can say or do

    Your child may hold up a hand and declare five at random moments — fingers out, very certain — and count stairs, snacks and fingers with fresh ambition. Watch for the double-tap: it is the next skill queueing up, not a flaw to fix.

    Out in the real world

    Fives frame the day: five toes on each foot at sock time, five candles to blow, five little pumpkins in the song, five minutes more at the park. Each five named is the anchor rehearsed.

    Try it together

    Finger-and-bug match: press your child’s hand on paper, trace it, and draw five ladybugs above the five fingertips — then let them draw a line from each bug to its finger. One-to-one counting as art, and the matching is the maths.

    Understanding check

    Ask tomorrow how many fingers one hand has — hands down first, then up for the count: a five that arrives before the wiggling starts means the number is carried in the head now, not just the hand.

    Parent tips

    End sessions at five without apology — a complete, happy five beats a frazzled ten every time. If the count drifts, park the ladybugs in a line first: straight rows keep counts honest and children calm.

    Staying safe

    Ladybug crafts keep glue and googly eyes above tasting height — small craft pieces wait for the no-mouths years. Real ladybugs stay admired on leaves, not in fists; five is for counting, never for keeping.

    This lesson pairs with the Five Ladybugs flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Numbers 1–10.

    LEARNING PATH LESSON · NUMBERS 1–10 · AGES 3–4 YEARS

    Six Stars — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

    This lesson pushes past the fingers: your child counts all the way to six, discovers the hand is full at five, and learns the trick that carries counting forward — six is five and one more, or three and three.

    What is this?

    Six is five and one more. On the card: six smiling yellow stars, the word six and a big teal numeral 6 — a sky’s worth of counting, arranged so the count can pause in the middle without losing its place.

    What does it mean?

    Six is the first number that overflows the hand, which makes it the first that truly needs counting practice. And it is the first with a split inside it — three and three — the seed of adding, discovered rather than taught.

    What does the child need to know?

    Your child needs: six is one more than a whole hand, each star gets one touch, and two counts of three can stack into one count of six. Losing the count mid-way is normal — restarting from one is the professional move.

    Why this matters

    Crossing the five-line is a real milestone: from here, counting is a skill practised rather than a fact noticed. The three-plus-three trick teaches composition — numbers inside numbers — years before any plus sign appears.

    What it teaches

    Counting past the hand, restarts after tangles (the true skill of this age), part-whole thinking in embryo, numeral recognition at 6, and the persistence longer counts quietly demand.

    Words to learn

    sixstarshandrowsmoretogether

    Say this to your child

    “"Six stars! We counted five on our hand — and here is one more: six! Let’s count three stars, then three more — three and three makes six! Can you twinkle six fingers? Every star gets its own gentle touch."”

    Step by step

    1. Show the card and ask how many stars are smiling on it — then count together, one touch per star, taking a breath at the halfway point.
    2. Count five on your hand first, then add one more star: five fingers and one extra makes six — the hand plus a little bit more.
    3. Play the split game: cover three stars, count three, uncover, count the rest, then count all six together. Three and three stack into six.
    4. Build six at the table: six blocks in two rows of three, counted into place one tap at a time — then knock one off and recount.
    5. Finish with six twinkles: fingers opening and closing one by one, both hands, ending on a big star-shaped stretch — six, the full sky.

    Look closer at the picture

    Look at the card together: how many smiling yellow stars are twinkling on it? Touch each star once as you count all the way to six. Where is the big numeral 6? Where is the word six?

    Ask your child

    "How many stars are on the card?" "Is six more than five — by how many?" "Can you count three and then three more?" "What happens if we take one star away?" "Can you make six with your fingers and one extra?" — questions that stack.

    What your child can say or do

    Your child may count to six with tremendous drama and land on a different number each performance. Praise the journey, then count it yourself slowly — the restart, not the result, is the skill being built at this exact station.

    Out in the real world

    Sixes live past the hand: six eggs in the box, six wheels on the big lorry, six cupcake cases in the tin, six legs on every insect in the garden. Count them slowly — six rewards careful pointing.

    Try it together

    Egg-box six: take a six-cup egg box and drop one pom-pom into each cup, counting as they land — a full box is six, and every cup holds exactly one. Then empty it and count them out again. Filling and emptying is the whole game.

    Understanding check

    Ask for six blocks tomorrow in one go: a counted, tapped, correct six means the hand-line has been crossed. A tangle at four or five means replay the split game — three, then three more, slowly.

    Parent tips

    Two rows of three are kinder than a scattered six — arrangement is scaffolding, not cheating. When a count tangles, breathe and begin again from one with a smile: restarting is the skill this card exists to teach.

    Staying safe

    Pom-poms and egg cups stay out of baby-sibling territory — the filling game happens at the table with a grown-up nearby. Craft stars get their small parts glued by grown-ups; tiny pieces wait for the older years.

    This lesson pairs with the Six Stars flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Numbers 1–10.

    LEARNING PATH LESSON · NUMBERS 1–10 · AGES 3–4 YEARS

    Seven Flowers — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

    This lesson takes counting into the wobble zone: seven is where confident counters start missing, doubling and drifting — and where the real skill, a happy restart, gets practised. The flowers are scattered wide, so every touch has to be earned.

    What is this?

    Seven is six and one more. On the card: seven pink flowers strewn from one side of the wide card to the other, the word seven and a big pink numeral 7 — a little garden that rewards slow, careful touring.

    What does it mean?

    Seven has a reputation, and it has earned it: past five, the counting brain has to hold a growing number in mind while the finger keeps working. The wobble is not a wall — it is the exact spot where the skill gets built.

    What does the child need to know?

    Your child needs: seven comes after six, each flower gets one touch, and tangles at seven are completely normal — every counter alive has wobbled here. A row of objects keeps count better than a pile, at any age.

    Why this matters

    The seven-wobble is where children first meet their own attention as a thing that can be helped: slow down, line them up, start again. Those three moves are the entire toolkit of accurate counting, learned on flowers.

    What it teaches

    Counting endurance past the glance zone, restart patience, organising scattered objects into lines, wide-format card handling, and the quiet confidence of surviving the famously wobbly number.

    Words to learn

    sevenflowerslineslowwobbleagain

    Say this to your child

    “"Seven flowers! Let’s walk through the garden slowly and touch each one — one, two, three, four, five... six... seven. Did we lose count? That happens to everyone! Line them up, start from one, and go again — seven careful touches for seven flowers."”

    Step by step

    1. Show the wide card and ask how many flowers bloomed on it — then tour the garden slowly, one touch per flower, no rushing the tour.
    2. If the count tangles, smile and begin again from one — model the restart like it is the best part of the game, because it is.
    3. Stand seven blocks or small pebbles in a row and count them left to right — the row shows where the count stopped and what is still to come.
    4. Draw seven flowers of your own, then let your child touch-count their paper garden — one slow tour, one touch per bloom.
    5. Finish with seven slow jumps — one per flower — and a deep breath at the end: seven is a marathon, and marathons end in a rest.

    Look closer at the picture

    Look at the card together: how many pink flowers are blooming on it — are they in a neat line, or scattered wide? Touch each one as you count to seven. Find the big numeral 7 and the word seven — this card lies sideways, which makes the garden feel extra wide.

    Ask your child

    "How many flowers are on the card?" "Is seven more than six — can you show me?" "Can we line up seven blocks in a row?" "What happens if we lose count?" "Can you jump seven slow jumps?" — answered with patience, blocks and gentle landings.

    What your child can say or do

    Your child may reach six and stall, or skip from five to eight with total confidence — both are the seven-wobble in action, and both deserve a cheerful recount rather than a sigh. Watch for the day seven lands clean: it is a genuine little triumph.

    Out in the real world

    Sevens take patience: seven days in the week named at bedtime, seven stairs counted on the way up, seven peas lined up on the plate. Slow counts, real objects — seven repays every bit of care it asks for.

    Try it together

    Flower line-up: seven paper flowers get arranged in a row by your child, then counted, then rearranged — tall to short, short to tall — and counted again each time. Ordering and counting in one garden bed.

    Understanding check

    Ask for seven of something tomorrow — seven pegs on the line, seven blocks in a tower: if the count arrives clean, the wobble has been crossed. If not, line the objects up first and tour them slowly together.

    Parent tips

    Never rush a seven — your pacing is the lesson. Rows beat piles every time, and the restart deserves a happy voice: children keep counting for years when tangles are treated as part of the game, not a verdict on it.

    Staying safe

    Small line-up objects — pebbles, buttons, beads — stay away from babies and mouths, and the block row gets built on the floor away from stairs. Sideways cards are for tables, not underfoot; counting happens seated or squatting, not stepping backwards.

    This lesson pairs with the Seven Flowers flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Numbers 1–10.

    LEARNING PATH LESSON · NUMBERS 1–10 · AGES 3–4 YEARS

    Eight Frogs — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

    This lesson counts with its whole body: eight frogs, four and four — and a hopping count that lets restless children do the number with their legs. Sitting still is optional here; counting is not.

    What is this?

    Eight is seven and one more — or four and four, which is easier to carry. On the card: eight green frogs, the word eight and a big blue numeral 8, each frog a station on the counting route.

    What does it mean?

    Eight is the first count that genuinely rewards splitting: four frogs here, four there, eight altogether. And frogs invite movement — hop-counting turns a table exercise into a whole-body game that busy bodies can actually finish.

    What does the child need to know?

    Your child needs: eight comes after seven, each frog gets one touch, and two groups can be counted one after the other. Moving while counting is a help, not a hindrance — hopping children are counting children.

    Why this matters

    The four-plus-four split is part-whole thinking in its friendliest clothes: two groups and their total. Children who discover that numbers can be taken apart and put back together have found the door that all later adding walks through.

    What it teaches

    Counting group by group, part-whole splitting (four and four), movement-plus-counting coordination, frog-leg gross motor work, and row-by-row organisation — the tidy grid doing its quiet teaching.

    Words to learn

    eightfrogsrowshopsplitaltogether

    Say this to your child

    “"Eight frogs — ribbit! Let’s count this row: one, two, three, four. And the other row: five, six, seven, eight! Four frogs and four frogs makes eight frogs. Now hop like a frog and count your jumps — one, two, three... all the way to eight!"”

    Step by step

    1. Show the card and ask how many frogs are waiting — then count them together, finishing one group before hopping to the next.
    2. Count it the split way: four frogs on one side, four on the other — four and four — then count all eight straight through. Two routes, same number.
    3. Hop the count: eight frog jumps across the rug, one number per hop, ribbit optional but likely. Land on each number like a lily pad.
    4. Build eight: four blocks here, four blocks there, then push them together and count the combined pond — eight, every time.
    5. Finish with a frog count-down: eight hops shrinking to one enormous final leap — the biggest frog in the pond wins a ribbit chorus.

    Look closer at the picture

    Look at the card together: how many green frogs are waiting on it, and where are they sitting? Touch each frog once as you count to eight. Find the big numeral 8 and the word eight — then find the frog with the widest smile, if you can agree on one.

    Ask your child

    "How many frogs are on the card?" "How many on each side?" "Can you hop eight times and count your hops?" "What is four and four more?" "Are the two sides even, or does one have more?" — answered with hops, counts and ribbits.

    What your child can say or do

    Your child may hop-count doorframes, hallways and garden paths, announcing eight at every eighth hop with genuine relief. Moving counters sometimes gain a hop or lose one — the card is the anchor to come back and check against.

    Out in the real world

    Eights show up in grids: eight plates in the cupboard stack, eight stairs to the landing, eight legs if you count the spider and its friend. Two little groups of anything is an invitation to count it the split way.

    Try it together

    Lily-pad grid: chalk or tape eight squares on the floor and hop one number per pad, saying the number as each foot lands. Backwards for the brave. The grid keeps the count honest; the hopping keeps the child in the game.

    Understanding check

    Ask tomorrow what four and four makes: if eight arrives without fingers touching the table, the split has sunk in. If not, rebuild the two block-groups and count the merge together — the pond needs refilling, that is all.

    Parent tips

    Follow the energy: hopping counts work at bathtime, in hallways, up hills. If attention fades mid-count, split the count instead of shortening it — four and four is a rest stop built into the number itself.

    Staying safe

    Hopping happens on rugs and grass, never tiles or stairs, with the hop-lane cleared of toys first. Real frogs stay watched from the bank, never handled — eight is for counting, and pond edges are for grown-up hands.

    This lesson pairs with the Eight Frogs flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Numbers 1–10.

    LEARNING PATH LESSON · NUMBERS 1–10 · AGES 3–4 YEARS

    Nine Balloons — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

    This lesson climbs the last hill before ten: nine balloons, three rows of three, counted patiently from top to bottom. Your child discovers that big numbers are just little groups holding hands — and that resting mid-count is allowed.

    What is this?

    Nine is eight and one more — or three rows of three, which is how the card shows it. On the card: nine red balloons standing in tidy columns, the word nine and a big orange numeral 9.

    What does it mean?

    Nine is big enough to need a plan: count a row, rest, count the next. Children learn here that long counts are stamina events — and that the layout on the card is a friend, holding the count steady when memory wobbles.

    What does the child need to know?

    Your child needs: nine comes after eight, each balloon gets one touch, and three rows of three can be counted one after another. Drifting away mid-count is allowed and normal — the balloons will wait, and so will the lesson.

    Why this matters

    Counting nine teaches strategy, not just sequence: choose a route, follow the rows, keep your place. That self-organisation is the bridge to ten and beyond — and spotting three-threes inside nine is multiplication seen from a very great distance.

    What it teaches

    Long-count stamina, route planning across a grid, three-plus-three-plus-three composition, patience with self and numbers, and the focus that a tidy layout quietly trains.

    Words to learn

    nineballoonsrowsthreestacktotal

    Say this to your child

    “"Nine balloons! Look how they stand — three rows of three. Count them with me: one, two, three... four, five, six... seven, eight, nine! Three balloons, three balloons, three balloons — and altogether, nine! Can you pop them? One clap each!"”

    Step by step

    1. Show the card and ask how many balloons floated onto it — then count them together, one row at a time, top to bottom.
    2. Count it again the stacked way: three balloons, then three more, then the last three — three little groups stacking into one big nine.
    3. Build nine: nine blocks in three rows of three, counted into place one tap per block — then tip one away and recount the drifting balloon.
    4. Rest mid-count on purpose: count a row, take a stretch, count the next. Long counts breathe — show your child that stopping is part of going on.
    5. Finish with nine pretend balloon-pops — one clap per balloon — and a big wow for the last: nine is a lot of balloons.

    Look closer at the picture

    Look at the card together: how many red balloons, and how many rows do they stand in? Touch each balloon once as you count to nine. Find the big numeral 9 and the word nine, floating up by the balloons.

    Ask your child

    "How many balloons are on the card?" "How many rows of three?" "What is three and three and three?" "Can you clap nine times without stopping?" "Is nine more than eight — by how much?" — answered with claps, rows and stamina.

    What your child can say or do

    Your child may count to nine with a wobble around six and a heroic recovery — or abandon ship at seven and return after a biscuit. Both days are successes: long counts are endurance sports, and endurance grows by coming back.

    Out in the real world

    Nines wait patiently in daily life: nine peas pushed around a plate, nine stairs to the half landing, nine sleeps until the weekend as measured by a small person. Big counts, real objects, slow pointing — nine rewards the effort.

    Try it together

    Balloon rows: tape three paper-column strips on the floor and let your child place three pom-poms on each, counting the threes, then the total. Nine placed, nine counted, nine clapped — a whole number line in one game.

    Understanding check

    Ask for the count on a nine-ish pile tomorrow — nine blocks, nine pegs: a routed, row-by-row count means the strategy landed. A scatter-count tangle means rebuild the rows first; the layout is the scaffold, so use it.

    Parent tips

    Teach the route, not just the numbers: top to bottom, left to right, finish a row before moving on. And let tired counters stop — the card waits, balloons wait, and returning tomorrow is how long counts are actually won.

    Staying safe

    Tape and paper rows stay flat on the floor, and pom-poms stay away from babies — the balloon game is table-or-floor with a grown-up in range. Real balloons are for grown-ups to blow up and tie, and popped bits go straight in the bin.

    This lesson pairs with the Nine Balloons flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Numbers 1–10.

    LEARNING PATH LESSON · NUMBERS 1–10 · AGES 3–4 YEARS

    Ten Butterflies — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

    This lesson reaches the summit: ten. Two rows of five butterflies, two hands of five fingers, one enormous celebration. Your child counts the whole set, meets their own two hands as the number they carry everywhere, and finishes the counting journey that started with one apple.

    What is this?

    Ten is nine and one more — and five and five, and a whole pair of hands. On the card: ten blue butterflies fluttering in a pair of rows, the word ten and a big green numeral 10 — the grand finale of the counting cards.

    What does it mean?

    Ten is the number children own twice: once on the card, once on their fingers. Matching butterflies to fingers one-to-one is the deepest work this card does — the count and the body agreeing, ten and ten, a whole system clicking together.

    What does the child need to know?

    Your child needs: ten comes after nine, each butterfly gets one touch, and ten matches both hands together. And the kindly secret: stopping at five on a tired day is a complete lesson, not an early finish.

    Why this matters

    Ten is the base of the whole number system — every bigger number is built from tens. A child who has counted ten slowly, matched it to ten fingers and celebrated reaching it has shaken hands with the structure of all future maths.

    What it teaches

    Two-digit recognition (the 1 and the 0 teaming up), ten-as-five-and-five, finger matching at full scale, celebration and pride — finishing a long journey is its own developmental event.

    Words to learn

    tenbutterflieshandsfingersallcelebrate

    Say this to your child

    “"Ten butterflies! Two rows of five — let’s count them all: one, two, three, four, five — and five more: six, seven, eight, nine, ten! Now your hands — one wiggle for every number we say. Ten butterflies, ten fingers! You counted the whole way. Hooray for ten!"”

    Step by step

    1. Show the card and ask how many butterflies arrived for the finale — then count them together, one row of five, then the other.
    2. Match the count to hands: five butterflies, five fingers on one hand; five more, five on the other — ten and ten, agreeing beautifully.
    3. Wiggle the count: one finger wiggles for every number said, all the way to ten, ending in two hands flung open — ten!
    4. Build the full set: line up all the number cards from one to ten and count the whole parade — the journey from one apple to ten butterflies, walked end to end.
    5. Finish with the drumroll: knees slapped fast, hands up, TEN! — and if the day was long, a five-high-five and see you tomorrow, because five is a finish line too.

    Look closer at the picture

    Look at the card together: how many blue butterflies are fluttering on it? What two digits make the big green numeral — a 1 and a 0? Touch each butterfly once as you count to ten, then hold up both hands and count their ten fingers too.

    Ask your child

    "How many butterflies are on the card?" "How many fingers do you have — all together?" "What is five and five more?" "Which card comes after nine?" "Can you count our whole number line from one?" — the grand-finale questions.

    What your child can say or do

    Your child may march through the whole number line unprompted, count ten stairs, ten peas and ten sleepy yawns, and demand the drumroll nightly. Ten becomes the badge of honour it deserves to be — worn loudly, with both hands.

    Out in the real world

    Tens close every day: ten toes in the bath, ten biscuits in the packet minus a few, ten goodnight kisses — one per finger, counted slowly. The whole set lives on the fridge now, counted front to back on proud mornings.

    Try it together

    The full parade: lay all ten number cards out in order and walk the line, touching each card and naming it — one apple, two ducks, all the way to ten butterflies. Then shuffle three cards and let your child put the parade back in order. The walk is the review; the fixing is the mastery.

    Understanding check

    Ask for ten tomorrow at bathtime — ten toes: if the count lands clean with a wiggle per toe, the finish line was truly crossed. Then flip it: ask what comes after nine, and listen for the two-digit answer arriving proudly.

    Parent tips

    Match every long count to the hands — five and five is the skeleton of ten, and fingers are always in stock. End tired days at five with full honours: the set rewards returning counters far more than it rewards stubborn ones.

    Staying safe

    Paper cards live on the fridge or at table height, not underfoot. Bathtime toe-counting happens seated with a grown-up within arm’s reach — and the drumroll is knee-slapped, never table-banged, for the sake of the dinner below.

    This lesson pairs with the Ten Butterflies flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Numbers 1–10.
